analysis.one_liner: Gives tenants in federally subsidized housing the right to form tenant organizations without landlord permission.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced with no cosponsors on December 15, 2022, referred to two House committees, and died without a vote when the 117th Congress ended three weeks later.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would give tenants in Section 8 voucher housing and Low-Income Housing Tax Credit buildings the legal right to form and run tenant organizations. Landlords and public housing agencies would have to recognize these groups, allow leafleting, door-knocking, and independent meetings without prior permission, respond in writing to tenant comments, and face a presumption of retaliation if they take adverse action against a tenant member. It would also fund grants for tenant outreach, training, and organizing support.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-income tenants who receive Section 8 vouchers or live in Low-Income Housing Tax Credit rent-restricted units. They would gain a federally protected right to organize — distribute leaflets, survey neighbors, hold independent meetings, and petition for better conditions — without needing landlord permission and with protection against retaliation, including a rule that any adverse action against a tenant-organizer is presumed retaliatory. The bill would also direct money to nonprofit groups that train and support tenant organizations, and allow housing agencies to spend $25 per unit per year on resident councils.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Tenants in Section 8 and tax-credit housing

how_it_helps.text: Gives tenants receiving Housing Choice Voucher (Section 8) assistance and tenants in Low-Income Housing Tax Credit rent-restricted units the right to establish, operate, and participate in a tenant organization to address their living conditions and tenancy terms.

Requires public housing agencies and building owners to recognize legitimate tenant organizations, allow protected activities (distributing leaflets, door-to-door contact, posting notices, and independent on-site meetings management cannot attend unless invited), and prohibits requiring tenants to get prior permission.
Bars retaliation against tenants for organizing and creates a rebuttable presumption that any adverse action against a tenant who belongs to a tenant organization is retaliation.

Directs HUD to build an enforcement protocol with independent investigation of abuse allegations, a complaint catalog, confidentiality, and a prohibition on cutting off rental assistance to a tenant while their complaint is open, plus quarterly public reports on complaint volume and response times.
Requires housing agencies to notify tenants annually of the right to organize during recertification and to add the right to the Section 10 tenancy addendum, so tenants know the protections exist.

Funds tenant capacity building: grants to qualified independent nonprofits for outreach and training, an interagency agreement of at least $1,000,000 with the Corporation for National and Community Service for tenant outreach, and authority for housing agencies to fund $25 per unit per year for elected resident councils.

analysis.who_pays: Owners of voucher-subsidized and tax-credit buildings and the public housing agencies that administer vouchers would bear new compliance duties: recognizing organizations, hosting or permitting organizing activity, answering tenant comments in writing within 60 days, and carrying the burden of proving that adverse actions against tenant-organizers were not retaliation. For LIHTC owners, compliance would be a condition of keeping the property's tax-credit status. Federal grant funding for tenant outreach and training would come from the Treasury.

drawbacks.text: The bill would impose real compliance costs and legal exposure on subsidized-housing owners and state housing credit agencies: required recognition of tenant groups, mandatory leafleting and meeting access, written responses to comments within 60 days, and a presumption of retaliation that owners would have to rebut. Critics would argue this raises the cost of participating in the voucher and LIHTC programs and could make some owners reluctant to house voucher holders.

Enforcement would be administrative and thin. The bill authorizes appropriations 'such sums as are necessary' but guarantees no money, so the complaint system, investigations, outreach notices, and grant program would depend entirely on future appropriations — leaving tenants with rights on paper but little recourse if underfunded.
The new grant spending and the $25-per-unit resident council funding would add federal outlays with no offsetting revenue in the bill.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The tenant protections are genuinely substantive — especially the anti-retaliation presumption, the ban on requiring permission to organize, and the rule against cutting off assistance to complainants — and the costs fall on landlords who already accept federal subsidies, which is a defensible trade. The honest weakness is enforcement: the bill creates rights and reporting requirements but leaves the money for enforcement and grants to future appropriations, so its real-world force would depend on Congress and HUD actually funding it.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in mid-December with zero cosponsors, sent to two House committees, and neither committee acted before Congress shut down three weeks later.

narrative.text: Rep. Andy Levin introduced the Tenants' Right to Organize Act in the House on December 15, 2022, near the end of the 117th Congress.
The bill was referred to the Financial Services Committee and, in addition, to the Ways and Means Committee; neither took it up.
No other member signed on as a cosponsor.
The 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, and the bill expired without a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Owners of Section 8 and tax-credit buildings and the public housing agencies that administer vouchers came out ahead: they avoid the organizing rights, anti-retaliation presumption, and written-response duties the bill would have imposed. Tenants in subsidized housing got nothing, and no comparable organizing right exists for them under this bill.

for.name: Rep. Andy Levin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the final weeks of the 117th Congress and recruited no cosponsors before it expired.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction and never scheduled a hearing or markup before the Congress ended.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Received a concurrent referral for the tax-credit provisions and took no action before the Congress ended.

against.name: House members generally
against.what_they_did: None joined as a cosponsor — no Republican and no additional Democrat signed on in the bill's three weeks of existence.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; the only recorded support was one Democratic sponsor with zero cosponsors from either party, so no partisan split can be measured.

industries.industry: Owners of Low-Income Housing Tax Credit properties
industries.note: The bill would make tenant-organizing rights a condition of keeping a project's tax-credit status: owners would have to recognize tenant organizations, allow leafleting and independent meetings without prior permission, respond to tenant comments, and rebut a presumption of retaliation for any adverse action against a tenant-organizer. This is the industry group the bill most directly regulates, since nearly all LIHTC tenants would gain the right to organize.

industries.industry: Private landlords renting to Section 8 voucher holders
industries.note: Every 'owner' of a unit occupied by a voucher tenant would face the same recognition, access, and anti-retaliation duties. Landlords who rely on voucher income would have to accept tenant organizing they can currently restrict or block.

Agencies would gain new duties — annual notice to tenants, written responses to tenant organizations within 60 days, and participation in the enforcement protocol — but also new money: authority to fund $25 per unit per year for elected resident councils.

industries.industry: Tenant organizing and housing nonprofit groups
industries.note: The bill would create a federal grant stream for nonprofits with organizing track records to do tenant outreach, training, and technical assistance, including a $1,000,000-plus interagency agreement for tenant outreach — a direct funding gain for the tenant-organizing field.
